human-information-processing.title: Human Information Processing
human-information-processing.content:
Chapter 3: Human Computer Interaction

HUMAN INFORMATION PROCESSING

Human Information Processing (HIP) studies how people receive, process, and respond to information. It connects psychology (how the brain works) and computer science (how machines process data).

  • Goal: Make technology easier, faster, and safer to use.
  • Human factors = understanding what people can and cannot do well
  • Designers must consider: Strengths: quick recognition, learning patterns. Limitations: memory lapses, slower reaction under stress.
  • Purpose: create systems that match human abilities.

TASK MODELING & PROBLEM-SOLVING MODEL

Task Modeling = step-by-step breakdown of how a user completes a task.

Problem-Solving Model:

  • Perception → recognizing information.
  • Cognition → analyzing and planning.
  • Action → executing response

HUMAN REACTION

Focuses on how fast and accurate humans can respond.

Influenced by:

  • Reaction time
  • Attention span
  • Error rate

IMPORTANCE IN HCI

  • Better interface design = improved user experience.
  • Reduces cognitive load and errors.
  • Enhances productivity and satisfaction

SUMMARY:

  • HIP = study of how humans handle information.
  • Human-factors knowledge helps create user-friendly systems.
  • Two main parts: 1. Task Modeling & Problem-Solving 2. Human Reaction & Performance Prediction
  • Application: Better apps, websites, and systems

sensation-and-perception-in-hci.title: Sensation and Perception in HCI
sensation-and-perception-in-hci.content:
Chapter 4: Human Computer Interaction

SENSATION AND PERCEPTION OF INFORMATION

  • Sensation: The process of detecting physical stimuli through the senses.
  • Perception: The process of interpreting and making sense of the sensation.
  • Key Idea: Sensation = input, Perception = meaning.
  • Users rely on senses to receive information from a system.
  • Perception helps them understand and act correctly.
  • Good design must consider: Clear visuals, Readable text, Meaningful icons and sounds

WHY IT MATTERS IN HCI

VISUAL PERCEPTION

  • The most dominant sense in HCI.
  • Important aspects: Color perception (contrast, color blindness). Size and visibility of objects. Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, continuity).
  • Example: Green = Go, Red = Stop. Icons grouped together are seen as related.

AUDITORY PERCEPTION

  • Hearing used for alerts, notifications, voice interaction.
  • Key aspects: Volume – must be noticeable but not irritating. Tone/Pitch – conveys urgency (high-pitch alarms = emergency). Recognition of patterns – familiar sounds are easier to identify.

Haptic (Touch) Perception

  • Users also process information through touch.
  • Includes: Vibration feedback (haptic feedback on phones). Force feedback (game controllers).
  • Improves immersion and interaction.

Limits of Sensory Perception

  • Visual overload – too much info on screen = confusion.
  • Auditory overload – too many notifications = irritation.
  • Individual differences – color blindness, hearing loss, or disability.
  • Design Tip: Keep interfaces simple, clear, and accessible.

SUMMARY

  • Sensation = raw input, Perception = interpretation.
  • In HCI, designers must consider: Vision (colors, shapes, grouping), Hearing (alerts, notifications), Touch (vibration, feedback)
  • Good design = information that is easy to sense and understand.
